arXiv:2512.07986v1 [math.AG] 08 Dec 2025

On germs of mappings ℂ2→ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2}

S. Yu. Orevkov Address: IMT, l’université de Toulouse, Toulouse, France Email address: orevkov@math.univ-toulouse.fr Address: Steklov Math. Institute, RAS, Moscow, Russia
Abstract.

We describe germs of mappings (ℂ2,0)→(ℂ2,0)(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^{2},0) ramified along a germ of irreducible curve whose image is of the form xp=yqx^{p}=y^{q}.

This paper is an addendum to Kulikov’s paper [6]. Theorem 4 in [6] describes germs of mappings (ℂ2,0)→(ℂ2,0)(\mathbb{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^{2},0) which have quadratic ramification along an irreducible germ of curve whose image has one characteristic pair. In the present paper we give another proof of this result (based on the techniques from [8, §1]) and generalize it to an arbitrary order of ramification.

Beside that, the extra property (see [6, п. 0.1]) is proven in §6 for a larger class of germs. Hence (see [6, Corollary 1]11 1 Theorem 5 in the arxiv version of the paper [6].) the results of [5] extend to this class. These results generalize the Chisini conjecture on sufficient conditions for a surface SS to be uniquely determined by the image of the ramification curve of a regular mapping S→ℂ​ℙ2S\to\mathbb{CP}^{2}.

I am grateful to Vik. S. Kulikov, M. G Zaidenberg, and A. K. Zvonkin for useful discussions and advise for improving the manuscript.

1. The main context

Let UU be an open ball in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} centered at the origin and CC be a curve ud1=vd2u^{d_{1}}=v^{d_{2}}, gcd​(d1,d2)=1\text{\rm gcd}(d_{1},d_{2})=1, min⁡(d1,d2)>1\min(d_{1},d_{2})>1. Let F:U~→UF:\widetilde{U}\to U be a covering of a finite degree NN, branched over CC. Let C~⊂U~\widetilde{C}\subset\widetilde{U} be the singular locus of FF (the set of points where FF is not a local diffeomorphism). Suppose that the following conditions hold.

  • (A1)

    U~\widetilde{U} is a domain in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, the mapping FF is analytic, and F⁡(0)=0F(0)=0;

  • (A2)

    the restriction of FF to each irreducible component of f−1​(C)f^{-1}(C) (in particular, to C~\widetilde{C}) is bijective.

Let nn be the order of ramification of FF along C~\widetilde{C}. This means that the divisor of the Jacobian of FF is (n−1)​C~(n-1)\widetilde{C}.

Let f:X~→Xf:\widetilde{X}\to X be a simple normal crossing model (SNC-model) of FF in the sense that σ:X→U\sigma:X\to U and σ~:X~→U~\widetilde{\sigma}:\widetilde{X}\to\widetilde{U} is a composition of blowups of the origin and its infinitely near points, σ−1​(C)\sigma^{-1}(C) is a simple normal crossing curve (SNC-curve), and f:X~→Xf:\tilde{X}\to X is a holomorphic mapping such that F∘σ~=σ∘fF\circ\widetilde{\sigma}=\sigma\circ f. We assume that the SNC-model is minimal, i.e. E:=σ−1​(0)E:=\sigma^{-1}(0) does not contain (−1)(-1)-curves whose valence in σ−1​(C)\sigma^{-1}(C) is 11 or 22 and E~:=σ~−1​(0)\widetilde{E}:=\widetilde{\sigma}^{-1}(0) does not contain (−1)(-1)-curves contracted by ff to a point.

It is well known that a minimal SNC-model exists and is unique up to equivalence. It can be obtained as follows. First, we construct an embedded SNC-resolution of the singularity of CC, and then resolve the indeterminacy points of FF by blowups on U~\widetilde{U}. We keep the notation CC and C~\widetilde{C} for the proper transforms of CC and C~\widetilde{C} on XX and X~\widetilde{X} respectively.

Given a compact SNC-curve D=D1+⋯+DkD=D_{1}+\dots+D_{k}, where the DiD_{i} are irreducible, denote

d(D)=det∥−Di⋅Dj∥i,j=1,…,k.d(D)=\det\|-D_{i}\cdot D_{j}\|_{i,j=1,\dots,k}.

We say that DD is a rational linear chain, if all the DiD_{i} are rational, Di⋅Di+1=1D_{i}\cdot D_{i+1}=1 for all ii, and Di⋅Dj=0D_{i}\cdot D_{j}=0 when |i−j|>1|i-j|>1. Then we call D1D_{1} and DkD_{k} the ends of DD.

Easy to see that EE is a rational linear chain. Let E0E_{0} be the component of EE that intersects CC, and let E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} be the closures of connected components of E∖E0E\setminus E_{0} (they are also rational linear chains). Denote the intersection points as follows: p0=E0∩Cp_{0}=E_{0}\cap C, pi=E0∩Eip_{i}=E_{0}\cap E_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2. It is well known (see, e.g., [4, ch. 5]) that d⁡(Ei)=did(E_{i})=d_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 (recall that C={ud1=vd2}C=\{u^{d_{1}}=v^{d_{2}}\}). This fact also immediately follows from [8, Prop. 1.5(d)] applied to the toric resolution (see, e.g., [2, §8.2]) of the singularity of CC.

2. Belyi functions and Zannier’s theorem

Denote the Riemann sphere ℂ∪{∞}\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\} by ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}}. We need the following result.

Theorem 1.

(Zannier [11, Theorem 1].) Let α=(α1,…,αk)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}) and β=(β1,…,βl)\beta=(\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{l}) be two tuples of positive integers such that ∑αi=∑βj=N\sum\alpha_{i}=\sum\beta_{j}=N, n:=k+l−1≤Nn:=k+l-1\leq N, and gcd​(α1,…,αk,β1,…,βl)=1\text{\rm gcd}(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k},\,\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{l})=1. Then there exists a rational function g:ℂ^→ℂ^g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}} with three critical values22 2 Such functions are called Belyi functions. with the sequences of multiplicities α,β\alpha,\beta, and (n,1,…,1)(n,1,\dots,1) at their preimages.

This theorem is proven in [11] in terms of products of permutations (see also [3]). A simple and elegant proof based on ‘‘dessins d’enfants’’ is given in [9, Theorem 3.3], [1, Theorem 3.3].

Remark 1.

In [9], Pakovich and Zvonkin found all the pairs (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) in Theorem 1 which define gg uniquely up to automorphisms of ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}}. In [10] they found an explicit form of gg for each such pair.

Remark 2.

Under the hypothesis of Theorem 1, one can choose coordinates on ℂ^\widehat{\mathbb{C}} such that 0,1,∞0,1,\infty are the critical values, (n,1,…,1)(n,1,...,1) are the multiplicities at g−1​(∞)g^{-1}(\infty), and nn is the multiplicity of ∞\infty. Then g=P/Qg=P/Q where P⁡(t)=∏(t−ai)αiP(t)=\prod(t-a_{i})^{\alpha_{i}}, Q⁡(t)=∏(t−bi)βiQ(t)=\prod(t-b_{i})^{\beta_{i}}, and deg⁡(P−Q)=N−n\deg(P-Q)=N-n. Such pairs of polynomials (P,Q)(P,Q) are called in [1, 10] Davenport–Zannier pairs (DZ-pairs).

3. The main lemma: an application of results from [8]

The definition and statements of results from [8, §1] are not presented here, because §1 of that paper is completely independent of the rest of the paper, moreover, the most of its content are definitions, notation, and statements.

Lemma 3.1.

(See Fig. 1.) There exists an irreducible component E~0\widetilde{E}_{0} of E~\widetilde{E} such that:

  • (i)

    E~0\widetilde{E}_{0} is the closure of f−1​(E∖(E1∪E2∪C))f^{-1}(E\setminus(E_{1}\cup E_{2}\cup C)).

  • (ii)

    f−1​(Ei)f^{-1}(E_{i}), i=1,2i=1,2, is a union of disjoint rational linear chains E~i(1),…,E~i(ℓi)\widetilde{E}_{i}^{(1)},\dots,\widetilde{E}_{i}^{(\ell_{i})}. Each chain E~i(j)\widetilde{E}_{i}^{(j)} transversally intersects E~0\widetilde{E}_{0} at a point pi(j)p_{i}^{(j)} which belongs to one of the ends of E~i(j)\widetilde{E}_{i}^{(j)}.

  • (iii)

    f−1​(p0)f^{-1}(p_{0}) is a finite set of points, one of which is p~0:=C~∩E~0\widetilde{p}_{0}:=\widetilde{C}\cap\widetilde{E}_{0} (recall that p0=E0∩Cp_{0}=E_{0}\cap C).

  • (iv)

    ff is not ramified along E~0\widetilde{E}_{0}.

  • (v)

    The numbers di(j):=d⁡(E~i(j))d_{i}^{(j)}:=d\big(\widetilde{E}_{i}^{(j)}\big) are positive, pairwise coprime, and at most two of them are greater than 11;

  • (vi)

    The restriction f|E~0f|_{\widetilde{E}_{0}} is a covering of degree NN ramified at the points pi(j)p_{i}^{(j)} and p~0\widetilde{p}_{0} (these points are defined in (ii), (iii)). Denote the order of ramification of f|E~0f|_{\widetilde{E}_{0}} at these points by mi(j)m_{i}^{(j)} and m0m_{0} respectively. Recall that nn is the order of ramification of ff along C~\widetilde{C}. Then:

    m1(1)+⋯+m1(ℓ1)=m2(1)+⋯+m2(ℓ2)=N,m0=n,m_{1}^{(1)}+\dots+m_{1}^{(\ell_{1})}=m_{2}^{(1)}+\dots+m_{2}^{(\ell_{2})}=N,\quad m_{0}=n, (3.1)
    ℓ1+ℓ2=n+1,\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}=n+1, (3.2)
    mi(j)di(j)=di,i=1,2,j=1,…,ℓi,m_{i}^{(j)}d_{i}^{(j)}=d_{i},\qquad i=1,2,\quad j=1,\dots,\ell_{i}, (3.3)
    N⁡(d1(1)​…​d1(ℓ1))​(d2(1)​…​d2(ℓ2))=d1​d2.N\left(d_{1}^{(1)}\dots d_{1}^{(\ell_{1})}\right)\left(d_{2}^{(1)}\dots d_{2}^{(\ell_{2})}\right)=d_{1}d_{2}. (3.4)
Proof.

(i)–(iv). If DD is a rational linear chain with negative definite intersection form and VV is the union of small tubular neighborhoods of its components, then π1​(V∖D)≅ℤd⁡(D)\pi_{1}(V\setminus D)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{d(D)} (see [7, §I]). Hence a proper analytic mapping of a smooth surface V~→V\widetilde{V}\to V which is a covering over V∖DV\setminus D is determined up to equivalence by its degree as soon as V~\widetilde{V} does not contain (−1)(-1)-curves. It is easy to derive from this fact that all such coverings are equivalent to mappings of toric surfaces described in [8, §1.4], whence Conditions (i)–(iv) follow.

Indeed, DD is defined by a fun Σ\Sigma which is the primitive subdivision of the cone spanned by the vectors (1,0)(1,0) and (e,d)(e,d), d=d⁡(D)d=d(D), gcd​(e,d)=1\text{\rm gcd}(e,d)=1 (see [8, Prop. 1.5(e)]). For each divisor mm of dd, consider the homomorphism A:ℤ2→ℤ2A:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{Z}^{2}, (x,y)↦(x,m​y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,my) and define Σ~\widetilde{\Sigma} as the primitive subdivision of the fan A−1​(Σ)A^{-1}(\Sigma). Then A∗:XΣ~→XΣA_{*}:X_{\widetilde{\Sigma}}\to X_{\Sigma} is a mapping of toric surfaces, which is a covering of degree mm over the complement of DD (see [8, Prop. 1.6]).

(v). The positivity of di(j)d_{i}^{(j)} follows from the negative definiteness of the intersection form. The fact that all of them, maybe except two, are equal to 11 can be proven by induction on the number of blowups, since d⁡(σ−1​(D))=d⁡(D)d(\sigma^{-1}(D))=d(D) when σ\sigma is a blowup of a point on an SNC-curve DD (see also [4, ch. 5]).

(vi). The equation (3.1) is evident; (3.2) follows from the Riemann–Hurwitz formula; (3.3) follows from [8, Prop. 1.6]; (3.4) follows from [8, Prop. 1.2].33 3 There is a misprint in [8, §1.2]: two different numbers are denoted by nn. It is corrected in the version of the paper available at https://www.math.univ-toulouse.fr/~orevkov/jci-e.pdf. ∎

Proof.

and F⁡(sk2,sk1)=(sd2,sd1)F(s^{k_{2}},s^{k_{1}})=(s^{d_{2}},s^{d_{1}}), i.e. FF is a covering branched over {ud1=vd2}\{u^{d_{1}}=v^{d_{2}}\} with ramification order nn along {xk1=yk2}\{x^{k_{1}}=y^{k_{2}}\}. It is easy to see that the point (1,0)(1,0) has NN preimages, hence the degree of FF is NN.

In order to find the parameters of the SNC-model, we decompose σ\sigma and σ~\widetilde{\sigma} as follows:

(II). Follows from Lemma 3.1. Indeed, in virtue of Condition (v), one of the following cases (a) or (b) takes place up to swapping d1↔d2d_{1}\leftrightarrow d_{2}.

(a). d1(1)=⋯=d1(ℓ1)=d2(3)=⋯=d2(ℓ2)=1d_{1}^{(1)}=\dots=d_{1}^{(\ell_{1})}=d_{2}^{(3)}=\dots=d_{2}^{(\ell_{2})}=1. Remark 3.

It is clear that the covering in Case (a) with k1=1k_{1}=1 is equivalent to the covering in Case (b) with k1=1k_{1}=1 and the same k2k_{2} (after an evident correction of l1l_{1} and l2l_{2}). The coverings also remain equivalent after swapping k1k_{1} with k2k_{2} in Case (a), and after swapping all the subscripts 1 and 2 in Case (b). One can get rid of this ambiguity by imposing the following additional restrictions: k1≤k2k_{1}\leq k_{2} (in both cases) and k1≥2k_{1}\geq 2 in Case (a). It is easy to check that all the covering became pairwise non-equivalent under these restrictions. The covering type ((a) or (b)) and the parameters k1,k2,l1,l2k_{1},k_{2},l_{1},l_{2} are also uniquely determined by the numbers d1d_{1}, d2d_{2}, NN, and nn (for example, Type (b) occurs when d1d_{1} divides NN).
